howto.title: How to read this paper
howto.intro:
This paper walks through what our teachers reported about how our standards are taught, from Kindergarten to Grade 12. It has eight parts: the whole school, the three grade bands, and the four subjects. Each part has three sections: Facts, Patterns, and Moving forward (questions for teams to take forward, and options for our part in the story).

**Where the numbers come from.** Every figure is computed from the ratings sheet of 9 November 2026 (2,166 standards, 2,709 ratings, last rating 8 November) and checked against the Vertical Alignment reports and findings decks.

**The three ratings.**

| Rating | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| Taught in depth | ALL classes in the grade consistently teach, reteach, review and assess the standard |
| Introduced / exposed | Anything in between: some classes, or taught briefly (for example, 3 of 5 classes) |
| Not taught | No class in the grade teaches it |

**Four things to hold in mind while reading.**

- The ratings are what teachers reported as taught across a whole grade. They are not a measure of what students know or can do, and they do not judge any teacher.
- "In depth" is all or nothing. Teams may have read that more or less strictly, so a low figure can reflect a stricter reading, not less teaching. Where this matters most, the paper says so. Where a team rated nothing in depth, we read it as careful use of an all-or-nothing scale, not as an absence of teaching.
- Each team rated its own subject's standards. Much literacy (vocabulary, academic language, speaking, writing, reading non-fiction) is also taught through Science and Social Studies, and that teaching may not show in the ELA ratings.
- Shares are of the main grade-level ratings (one standard in one grade). Essential Elements (the alternate standards) are counted apart.

**We cannot teach everything equally.** No school can take every standard to depth, and that is not the goal. The goal is to choose on purpose: which standards we teach in depth, which we introduce, and which we leave out, and to plan that proportion together across the grades. The ratings show the mix we have now, so we can decide the mix we want.

**Instructional capacity.** How many standards a grade actually takes to depth, introduces or leaves out in a year, worked out from the ratings (the average for one grade). It is not a target and not a judgement: it describes what our teaching time holds now, so we can decide together how to use it.

**Categories.** In every part, each section groups its items under the same categories, in the same order, so a team can follow one kind of observation across the whole school, its band and its subject. Facts: Bright spots, Gaps, Breadth without depth, Anomalies and Other notable. Patterns: Trends across the grades, Handoffs, Language and literacy, How we rated, Choices and capacity, Toward the SAT and Other notable. Moving forward: Improving the curriculum, Working across grade levels, Knowing the bands above and below, and How we rate and plan. A category with nothing in it is left out.

**How each part is laid out.** Three sections, each opening with a small map that shows where you are: Facts, then Patterns, then Moving forward (questions to ponder, then options for our part in the story: improving the curriculum, working across grade levels, knowing the bands above and below, and a concrete action). Every pattern carries its figures in the text, and every question ends with the data behind it, in brackets and italics. The questions are invitations, not conclusions. Our strengths are named alongside the places where we might build.

whole.title: Part 1. The whole school, K-12
whole.intro:
Across K-12, teachers reported that 63% of our grade-level ratings are at least introduced, and 23% are taught in depth. Every team rated every standard it was asked about, which gives us a complete picture to work from for the first time.

|  | Rated | In depth | Introduced | Not taught |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| All subjects | 1,754 | 23% | 40% | 37% |
| Math | 460 | 17% | 45% | 38% |
| ELA | 652 | 35% | 44% | 21% |
| Science | 247 | 35% | 23% | 42% |
| Social Studies | 395 | 4% | 36% | 60% |

items.title: ELA carries more than half of all depth.
items.text: 227 of the 406 in-depth ratings are ELA (56%).

items.title: Where depth is highest.
items.text: Science Grade 10 (79% in depth), ELA Grade 2 (71%), ELA Grade 7 (70%), Math Grade 2 (62%), and ELA Grades 11 and 12 (60% each).

items.title: Progressions.
items.text: Of 155 progressions of linked standards, 59 break down on an official link, and 8 are taught at every step (at least introduced in each grade, not necessarily in depth).

items.title: Hand-overs between schools.
items.text: 46 standards are taught in depth while a standard they build on, placed in an earlier school, is rated not taught. Only 3 of these (all Math) rest on an official link; the other 43 rest on suggested links, not official ones, so each is worth checking first.

items.title: Standards no grade teaches.
items.text: 281 standards are rated not taught by every grade that could teach them. A further 172 are not taught where they were placed, with other grades not asked.

items.title: Coverage is steady by band.
items.text: The share at least introduced is 63% in K-5, 61% in 6-8 and 63% in 9-12. By grade it ranges from 37% (Grade 3) to 78% (Grade 1).

items.title: Introduced, never in depth.
items.text: 581 standards are introduced in at least one grade and in depth in none (Math 186, ELA 241, Science 49, Social Studies 105).

items.title: Fifteen grade-and-subject combinations have not yet rated a standard in depth.
items.text: Math in Grades 3, 6, 7 and 8; ELA in Kindergarten and Grade 3; Science in Grade 1; Social Studies in Grades 1, 2, 3, 4, 8, 9, 10 and 12. Each is a place to start a conversation, not a judgement: these teams may simply have read "in depth" most strictly.

items.title: Depth by grade swings widely.
items.text: From 55% in Grade 2 to 2% in Grade 3, then between 12% and 34% for every grade from Grade 4 to Grade 12.

items.title: Every rating is in.
items.text: All 1,754 grade-level ratings and all 955 Essential Element ratings were completed: 2,709 in all, with nothing left unrated.

items.title: "Introduced" is our most common rating.
items.text: 406 ratings are in depth (23%), 693 introduced (40%) and 655 not taught (37%). "Introduced" is the most common answer in the school.

items.title: Depth by band.
items.text: 21% in depth in K-5, 20% in 6-8 and 28% in 9-12.

items.title: Depth by subject.
items.text: ELA and Science lead at 35% each. Math is at 17% and Social Studies at 4%.

items.title: Our named priorities.
items.text: Of the 952 ratings on standards our own documents name as priority or power, 29% are in depth, 45% introduced and 26% not taught.

items.title: Essential Elements.
items.text: 43% of Essential Element ratings are in depth, against 23% for the main standards.

items.title: By band, coverage is steady and depth is not.
items.text: Every band introduces about the same share (61% to 63%), although by grade it ranges from 37% to 78%. What changes from grade to grade is how many of those are taken to depth. Our question is less "what are we missing?" and more "what do we choose to go deep on?"

items.title: Depth does not climb with grade.
items.text: Grade 2 (55%) is the highest grade in the school. High school is highest as a band (28%), but Grade 12 (23%) sits level with Grade 5 (24%).

items.title: Each subject has its own shape.
items.text: ELA rises from 19% in K-5 to 53% and 51% in the secondary bands. Science rises to 48% in high school. In middle school, Math introduces almost everything and has not yet rated a standard in depth. Social Studies stays between 3% and 6% throughout.

items.title: Both changes of school show a jump, in different directions.
items.text: From Grade 5 to Grade 6, Math falls (32% to 0%) while ELA rises (18% to 40%). From Grade 8 to Grade 9, Math rises (0% to 30%) while ELA falls (50% to 33%) and Science falls (43% to 17%).

items.title: Progression findings gather at 3 grades.
items.text: Grade 6 (29 findings), then Grades 2 and 5 (24 each). Grade 6 is where middle school standards meet what K-5 taught.

items.title: There is little repetition between grades.
items.text: No standard is flagged as a likely duplication. 37 standards are in depth in 2 or more grades of their own band, 34 of them in high school ELA. Grades 11 and 12 gave identical ratings on all 47 shared ELA standards, which is worth confirming.

items.title: "Introduced" is our usual rating.
items.text: In Math and ELA, 44% to 45% of ratings are introduced. This may fit a school where students learn language and content together, and where teaching often needs to be supported and revisited before it can be assessed for every class.

items.title: Essential Elements are rated in depth far more often in K-5.
items.text: 56% of K-5 Essential Elements are in depth against 21% of the main standards. This may show where much of our real teaching sits, or it may show that teams rated the support they give.

items.title: Essential Elements are rated far above the main standards in several grades.
items.text: In depth, main standards against Essential Elements: Grade 1 21% against 74%, Grade 2 55% against 75%, Grade 3 2% against 64%, Grade 5 24% against 73%. Only Grade 9 is lower (24% against 19%). Much deep teaching may be happening at the level students are at.

items.title: Literacy lives in every subject.
items.text: ELA is rated by ELA teams, yet much vocabulary, academic language, speaking and non-fiction reading is taught through Science and Social Studies. The 2026 literacy audit of weekly plans found about two-fifths of vocabulary teaching, speaking and non-fiction in those subjects. ELA's thinner strands (Language 10% in depth in K-5) may be taught more than the ELA ratings show.

items.title: Grade 2 and Grade 3 rated very differently.
items.text: Grade 2 (55% in depth) is 10 points or more above its subjects' averages in Math, ELA and Science. Grade 3 (2%) is 10 points or more below in the same three. When a whole grade moves together, the cause is more likely shared (how the scale was read, time, staffing) than any one subject.

items.title: Science is often all or nothing.
items.text: Only 23% of Science ratings are "introduced", half the rate of Math and ELA. One possible reason is that Science is planned in whole units. Grades 1, 4 and 9 are exceptions.

items.title: Priority standards are deeper in secondary; in K-5 they are level.
items.text: Priority standards are in depth more often than all standards in 6-8 (32% against 20%) and 9-12 (38% against 28%). In K-5 the power standards (20%) are level with all standards (21%). The ratings cannot tell us whether naming a standard made the difference, or whether teams named what they already teach in depth.

items.title: We cannot teach everything equally, so the mix should be a choice.
items.text: Today our mix is 23% in depth, 40% introduced and 37% not taught. The question is not how to make every standard "in depth", but whether this is the mix we would choose, and whether the right standards sit in each group.

items.title: Capacity shows what a grade carries in a year.
items.text: On average a grade takes about 31 standards to depth in a year across its four subjects (about 8 per subject), introduces about 53 and does not teach about 50, out of about 135 rated. By band, a grade takes about 25 standards to depth in K-5, 32 in 6-8 and 41 in 9-12. By subject, a grade takes about 17 ELA standards to depth a year, 7 Science, 6 Math and 1 Social Studies. This is a realistic picture of what we manage now, and a starting point for deciding what to protect. As shares of each subject's standards: ELA 35% in depth, 44% introduced, 21% not taught; Math 17% in depth, 45% introduced, 38% not taught; Science 35% in depth, 23% introduced, 42% not taught; Social Studies 4% in depth, 36% introduced, 60% not taught. Capacity here means how many standards a grade's teaching time actually holds in a year. It is not a target and not a judgement.

items.title: Grades 6, 8 and 12 carry the most standards.
items.text: Grade 8 rated 164 grade-level standards and Grades 6 and 12 rated 163 each, against 103 in Kindergarten. Middle school Social Studies alone asks each grade to rate 64.

items.title: Improving the curriculum
items.text: We could agree which standards we would protect in every grade if time ran short. A short, shared K-12 list of standards every class takes to depth could give the rest of the curriculum a spine.
items.data: 23% of ratings are in depth; 40% are introduced

items.text: Neighbouring grades could meet once a term to rate 5 shared standards together, and we could compare what "in depth" means.

k-5.title: Part 2. Elementary, K-5
k-5.intro:
In K-5, teachers reported that 63% of the 700 grade-level ratings are at least introduced, and 21% are taught in depth. Grade 2 has the highest share in depth of any grade, and Math and Science lead the band at 29% each.

| Share in depth | K | G1 | G2 | G3 | G4 | G5 | K-5 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Math | 26% | 42% | 62% | 0% | 21% | 32% | 29% |
| ELA | 0% | 21% | 71% | 0% | 7% | 18% | 19% |
| Science | 46% | 0% | 50% | 11% | 24% | 44% | 29% |
| Social Studies | 40% | 0% | 0% | 0% | 0% | 10% | 6% |
| All subjects | 16% | 21% | 55% | 2% | 12% | 24% | 21% |

items.title: Grade 2 has the most in depth.
items.text: 55% in depth across all subjects: ELA 71%, Math 62%, Science 50%.

items.title: Place value is our strongest Math strand.
items.text: 60% of Number and Operations in Base Ten ratings are in depth, including every Grade 2 standard.

items.title: Fractions are the thinnest Math strand.
items.text: None of the 30 fractions ratings in Grades 3 to 5 is in depth, and 63% are not taught.

items.title: Social Studies.
items.text: 64% of ratings are not taught. Only Kindergarten (40%) and Grade 5 (10%) have anything in depth. A further 24 Social Studies standards are not taught in the grade where they were placed.

items.title: Progressions.
items.text: 39 of 109 K-5 progressions break down on an official link. 18 are taught at every step, 11 of them in Science.

items.title: Standards no grade teaches.
items.text: 222 in K-5: ELA 100, Math 60, Social Studies 38, Science 24.

items.title: Grade 1 introduces the most.
items.text: 78% of Grade 1 standards are at least introduced, the highest of any grade K-12.

items.title: Introduced, never in depth.
items.text: 294 standards are introduced and never in depth: ELA 174, Math 63, Social Studies 29, Science 28.

items.title: Power lists.
items.text: Kindergarten names 47 of its 57 ELA standards as power standards, and Grade 3 rates 17 of its 18 Math power standards not taught.

items.title: Grade 3 rated differently.
items.text: 2% in depth and 63% not taught. In Math, 31 of 32 standards are rated not taught.

items.title: The band in 3 numbers.
items.text: 148 ratings in depth (21%), 295 introduced (42%), 257 not taught (37%).

items.title: By subject.
items.text: Math 29% in depth, Science 29%, ELA 19%, Social Studies 6%.

items.title: ELA strands.
items.text: Reading Foundational Skills and Speaking and Listening are at 25% in depth, Reading 24%, Writing 22%, Language 10%.

items.title: Science strands.
items.text: Life Science 47% in depth, Physical Science 31%, Earth and Space 25%, Engineering 11%.

items.title: Power standards.
items.text: 20% of power standard ratings are in depth and 37% are not taught, level with all standards (21%).

items.title: Essential Elements.
items.text: 56% in depth: Math 82%, ELA 46%. K-5 Science and Social Studies use AERO and have no Essential Elements.

items.title: Social Studies starts well and fades.
items.text: Kindergarten has 40% in depth. Grades 1 to 4 have not yet rated a Social Studies standard in depth, and Grades 2, 3 and 4 rate 73% to 89% not taught, perhaps because much of that time goes to literacy.

items.title: Science depth alternates by year.
items.text: In depth by grade: 46%, 0%, 50%, 11%, 24%, 44%. Coverage does not alternate: Grade 1 introduces 75% of its Science standards. One possible reason is that each year runs different units.

items.title: K-2 builds; Grade 3 rated very differently.
items.text: Depth climbs from 16% in Kindergarten to 21% and 55%, is 2% in Grade 3 (a grade that rated most of its Essential Elements in depth), and rebuilds to 12% and 24%. The Grade 3 dip appears in Math, ELA and Science.

items.title: Number is strong, and the path beyond number is thin.
items.text: Place value reaches 60% in depth. Operations and Algebraic Thinking (23%, with 43% not taught), Measurement and Data (23%) and Fractions (0%) are the strands that lead into middle school Math.

items.title: Physical Science in K-5 matters later.
items.text: Twelve Physical Science standards are taught by no K-5 grade. Nine of the 17 Science hand-over gaps start here and feed Grade 8 and Grade 10 Physical Science, which are among our strongest results.

items.title: Six Math progressions break down.
items.text: Counting, place value, addition and subtraction, multiplication and division, measurement, and area and volume each have a step taught in depth above a step rated not taught.

items.title: Depth shifts by subject at the hand-over to Grade 6.
items.text: 34 hand-over gaps begin in K-5 (Science 17, ELA 12, Social Studies 5). From Grade 5 to Grade 6, Math goes from 32% to 0%, ELA from 18% to 40%, Science from 44% to 24%.

items.title: Kindergarten introduces widely in Math and Science but not yet in ELA.
items.text: Kindergarten has not yet rated an ELA standard in depth, and 93% of its Language standards are not taught. Speaking and Listening is the exception: every standard is introduced.

items.title: Language is thin even in our strongest grade.
items.text: Grade 2 Language is 31% in depth while every other Grade 2 ELA strand is 78% to 100%.

items.title: Grade 3 may be teaching at the level students are at.
items.text: Grade 3 rated most of its Essential Elements in depth (Math 59%, ELA 66%) and kept "in depth" for none of its grade-level standards. Grades 1 and 5 show the same pattern more mildly (Essential Elements 74% and 73% in depth against 21% and 24%). One reading: teams teach in depth at the level students are at, and kept "in depth" for the grade-level standard itself.

items.title: Language holds many of the ELA standards no grade teaches.
items.text: Language has 43 of the 100 ELA standards no grade teaches, and 52 of the 174 that are only introduced.

items.title: Literacy is also taught through Science and Social Studies.
items.text: K-5 classes teach vocabulary, talk and non-fiction reading inside Science and Social Studies units, which the ELA ratings may not capture. K-5 Science reaches 29% in depth, above K-5 ELA (19%).

items.title: Grade 2 and Grade 3 are 53 points apart.
items.text: That is the largest gap between neighbouring grades in the school. A gap this size is worth a conversation before either number is read as teaching.

items.title: Power standards are not yet our most secure.
items.text: In Social Studies, 68% of power standard ratings are not taught. In ELA, 18% are in depth.

items.title: Capacity shows what a K-5 grade carries in a year.
items.text: A K-5 grade takes about 25 standards to depth across its four subjects (about 6 per subject), introduces about 49 and does not teach about 43, out of about 117 rated. The range is wide, from 63 in depth in Grade 2 to 2 in Grade 3, where the team rated most cautiously. By subject, per grade: ELA about 11 in depth of 57 rated, Math 8 of 29, Science 4 of 15, Social Studies 1 of 16. As shares of each subject's standards: ELA 19% in depth, 51% introduced, 29% not taught; Math 29% in depth, 36% introduced, 35% not taught; Science 29% in depth, 32% introduced, 39% not taught; Social Studies 6% in depth, 30% introduced, 64% not taught. Capacity here means how many standards a grade's teaching time actually holds in a year. It is not a target and not a judgement.

g6-8.title: Part 3. Middle school, Grades 6-8
g6-8.intro:
In Grades 6-8, teachers reported that 61% of the 479 grade-level ratings (336 standards; each grade rates the same 64 Social Studies standards) are at least introduced, and 20% are taught in depth. ELA is the clear strength at 53%, with Grade 7 ELA at 70%.

| Math | 0% | 0% | 0% | 0% |
| ELA | 40% | 70% | 50% | 53% |
| Science | 24% | 10% | 43% | 27% |
| Social Studies | 6% | 3% | 0% | 3% |
| All subjects | 17% | 22% | 21% | 20% |

items.title: ELA leads.
items.text: 53% in depth, 29% introduced, 18% not taught. Writing (59%), Speaking and Listening (58%), Reading (52%) and Language (45%) are all strong.

items.title: Grade 7 Reading stands out.

items.title: Middle school Math rated almost everything introduced.
items.text: Almost every Math standard (71 of 81 ratings) is rated the same way, "introduced", in all three grades. A pattern that uniform is unusual. One possibility is a strict reading of "ALL classes, all or nothing". The team can tell us.

items.title: Grade 7 Social Studies rated most standards not taught.

items.title: Science looks organised by discipline.
items.text: Grade 6 carries Earth and Space (67% in depth). Grade 8 carries Physical Science (62%) and Engineering (100%). Life Science sits mainly in Grade 7 (15%). Standards placed in a grade that teaches a different discipline show as "not taught".

items.title: Priority standards are deepest where teaching is already deep.
items.text: ELA priority standards are in depth 68% of the time, above ELA as a whole (53%). In Math and Social Studies, priority standards are rated the same as everything else.

items.title: So Science "not taught" may mean "taught in another grade".
items.text: The 29 Science standards not taught where placed were placed by suggestion. This is a placement question before it is a gap.

items.title: Capacity shows what a middle school grade carries in a year.
items.text: A middle school grade takes about 32 standards to depth across its four subjects (about 8 per subject), introduces about 65 and does not teach about 63, out of about 160 rated, the most standards per grade of any band. items.title: ELA and Math move in opposite directions.
items.text: ELA depth nearly doubles from Grade 9 to Grade 12 (33% to 60%). Math depth falls from 30% to 6% over the same years.

items.title: Grades 9 and 10 build; Grades 11 and 12 match exactly.
items.text: Grades 9 and 10 rate the same 43 ELA standards but agree on only 18: Grade 9 introduces and Grade 10 deepens, like a two-year sequence. Grades 11 and 12 gave identical ratings on all 47 shared standards (28 in depth in both), which is worth confirming.

items.title: Grade 9 is a landing year.
items.text: ELA falls from 50% in Grade 8 to 33%, and Science from 43% to 17%, while Math rises from 0% to 30%. Grade 9 Writing is at 15% against 77% in Grade 10.

items.title: Language is the thinnest ELA strand again.
items.text: 30% in depth, against 54% to 69% for the other strands. It is also the thinnest strand in K-5 (10%).

items.title: Essential Elements in Social Studies outpace the main standards.
items.text: 22% in depth against 3%. In Science they are also slightly ahead (55% against 48%).

items.title: Science and Social Studies carry literacy too.
items.text: High school Science (48% in depth) uses reading, data and argument writing that ELA standards describe. Social Studies inquiry (all 10 standards not taught in Grades 9 and 10) may be close to the research ELA teaches in depth.

items.title: Priority Math is deepest in Grades 9 and 10.
items.text: In Grade 9, 75% of priority Math standards are in depth, and in Grade 10, 41%. In Grades 11 and 12 the figure is 13% and 9%.

items.title: "Not taught" often means "not in this course".
items.text: High school standards were placed in courses by suggestion. The 119 standards not taught where placed may be taught in another year, or belong to a course few students take. This is worth settling before anything is called a gap.

items.title: Science depth follows the course map.
items.text: Grade 10 is Physical Science (100% in depth), Grade 11 is Life Science (50%), Grade 9 is Earth and Space (21%). Grade 9 is the quietest Science year at 17%.

Capacity here means how many standards a grade's teaching time actually holds in a year. It is not a target and not a judgement.

items.text: Grade 9 equations and functions are the strongest part of high school Math. The SAT's other areas are thinner: data and statistics strands are at or near 0%, and geometry and trigonometry sit under 10% apart from Congruence (31%).

math.title: Part 5. Math, K-12
math.intro:
Across K-12, teachers reported that 62% of the 460 Math ratings (406 standards) are at least introduced, and 17% are taught in depth. Math has real peaks: Grade 2 (62% in depth), place value in K-5 (60%) and Grade 9 equations (60%).

|  | Rated | In depth | Introduced | Not taught |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| K-5 | 173 | 29% | 36% | 35% |
| 6-8 | 81 | 0% | 88% | 12% |
| 9-12 | 206 | 14% | 35% | 51% |
| K-12 | 460 | 17% | 45% | 38% |

items.title: Grade 4 Geometry and Grade 2 Operations are fully in depth.
items.text: Both are at 100%.

items.title: Place value is the strongest strand.
items.text: Number and Operations in Base Ten is 60% in depth in K-5: 100% in Grade 2, 75% in Grade 5, 63% in Grade 1.

items.title: Grade 9 equations.
items.text: Reasoning with Equations and Inequalities 60% in depth, Creating Equations 50%, The Real Number System 100%.

items.title: K-2 climbs steadily.
items.text: 26%, 42%, 62%: the clearest upward run in any subject.

items.title: Fractions.
items.text: 0% in depth across Grades 3 to 5. Not taught: 100% in Grade 3, 42% in Grade 4, 64% in Grade 5.

items.title: Progressions.
items.text: 10 of 18 Math progressions break down on an official Coherence Map link (a published map of which Math standards build on which). One, ratios and proportional relationships, is taught at every step.

items.title: Hand-overs.
items.text: Three Grade 9 standards taught in depth build on a Grade 6 or Grade 8 standard rated not taught. All 3 rest on official links.

items.title: Standards no grade teaches.
items.text: 70 confirmed: 60 in K-5 and 10 in 6-8, none in high school. Most are in Fractions (19), Operations and Algebraic Thinking (15) and Measurement and Data (15).

items.text: 77 high school standards, in courses where they were placed by suggestion.

items.text: 71 of 81 ratings are introduced, and none is yet rated in depth.

items.title: Depth by grade.
Priority and power standards.
items.text: 21% in depth, 61% introduced, 18% not taught. Grade 9 priorities are 75% in depth and Grade 2 power standards 64%.

items.title: Math dips in middle school, with strong ground on both sides.
items.text: Depth rises through K-2 (26%, 42%, 62%), recovers in Grades 4 and 5 (21%, 32%), rests at "introduced" for three years, and returns in Grade 9 (30%). The middle school years connect two places where we already teach deeply.

items.title: We are strongest in number, thinner in what number leads to.
items.text: Counting and place value are solid (place value is 60% in depth). Fractions, ratios, and expressions and equations, the strands that carry students from arithmetic to algebra, are not yet rated in depth from Grade 3 to Grade 8.

items.title: Fractions are the single clearest thread to follow.
items.text: Not in depth in Grades 3 to 5 (0 of 30 ratings), followed by ratios and proportional relationships introduced only in Grades 6 and 7 (6 of 6), followed by Grade 9 equations (60% in depth). Each depends on the one before.

items.title: Grade 3 is a hinge year.
items.text: Multiplication, division, fractions and area all begin in Grade 3. Six progression findings land there, the most of any grade in Math, and 4 of the 10 broken Math progressions trace back to Grade 3 standards rated not taught.

items.title: Kindergarten gaps are foundational ones.
items.text: Among the 60 K-5 standards no grade teaches are counting to 100, addition and subtraction word problems, and composing and decomposing numbers within 10. Grade 1 then teaches standards in depth that build on them.

items.title: K-5 Essential Elements tell a second story.
items.text: 82% of K-5 Math Essential Elements are in depth (95% in Grades 1 and 5). Much deep Math teaching may be happening at the Essential Element level, which the main ratings do not show.

items.title: In middle school the two sets agree.
items.text: Essential Elements are also almost all "introduced" in Grades 6 to 8 (7% in depth). That consistency again points to how "in depth" was read.

items.title: The dip may be partly how the scale was read.
items.text: Middle school Math (71 of 81 ratings) is rated almost uniformly "introduced", and Grade 3 (31 of 32) almost uniformly "not taught". Uniform ratings across a whole grade usually say more about the reading of the scale than about each standard.

items.title: High school Math narrows by design or by default.
items.text: 51% is not taught, and whole strands (vectors, complex numbers, trigonometric functions, probability for decisions) have little or nothing. Several of these are advanced strands not every pathway includes. Whether that is a choice is worth saying out loud.

items.title: Priority standards are deeper in high school.
items.text: Priority standards are in depth at almost twice the rate of all high school Math standards (27% against 14%): 75% in Grade 9, but 13% and 9% in Grades 11 and 12.

items.title: Capacity shows what a grade carries in Math each year.
items.text: A grade takes about 6 Math standards to depth a year, introduces about 16 and does not teach about 14, out of about 35 rated. In K-5 it is about 8 of 29, in middle school none yet of 27 (24 introduced), in high school about 7 of 52. As shares of Math standards: K-5 29% in depth, 36% introduced, 35% not taught; 6-8 0% in depth, 88% introduced, 12% not taught; 9-12 14% in depth, 35% introduced, 51% not taught. Capacity here means how many standards a grade's teaching time actually holds in a year. It is not a target and not a judgement.

items.title: On the SAT road, algebra is our strongest area.
items.text: Algebra is our strongest high school area (about 28% in depth). Data analysis (about 3%) and geometry and trigonometry (about 7%) are thinner, and in middle school all of these are introduced only.

items.title: Only 3 standards are in depth in more than one grade.
items.text: Creating equations, function notation and solving equations are each in depth in 2 or 3 high school grades. They are also the core of SAT algebra.

ela.title: Part 6. ELA, K-12
ela.intro:
Across K-12, teachers reported that 79% of the 652 ELA ratings (562 standards) are at least introduced, the widest coverage of any subject, and 35% are taught in depth. ELA accounts for more than half of all the in-depth teaching in the school, and Science and Social Studies carry more literacy teaching than these ratings show.

|  | Rated | In depth | Introduced | Not taught |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| K-5 | 340 | 19% | 51% | 29% |
| 6-8 | 132 | 53% | 29% | 18% |
| 9-12 | 180 | 51% | 42% | 8% |
| K-12 | 652 | 35% | 44% | 21% |

items.title: Three peaks.
items.text: Grade 2 (71%), Grade 7 (70%) and Grades 11 and 12 (60%).

items.title: Grade 2 in detail.
items.text: Writing 100% in depth, Speaking and Listening 88%, Reading Foundational Skills 80%, Reading 78%.

items.title: ELA is the school's success story in the making.
items.text: Depth roughly triples from K-5 (19%) to secondary (53% and 51%), and "not taught" shrinks from 29% to 8%. By high school almost every ELA standard is met.

items.title: The build is not a straight line.
items.text: Grade 2 (71%) is followed by Grade 3 (0%) and Grade 4 (7%). Grade 8 (50%) is followed by Grade 9 (33%). The Grade 9 dip follows the move to high school. The Grade 3 dip has no such change, which makes it worth a closer look.

items.title: Middle school is where progressions strain.
items.text: Twelve of 29 progressions break down in Grades 6 to 8, usually where a middle school standard in depth builds on a K-5 step rated not taught. Reading and research skills (text features, evidence for claims, inquiry projects) recur.

items.title: Grades 9 and 10 look like a two-year sequence.
items.text: They rate the same 43 standards but agree on only 18: Grade 9 introduces and Grade 10 deepens. Grades 11 and 12 rate all 47 shared standards identically.

items.title: Language is the thread that never fully catches up.
items.text: It is the thinnest strand in every band (10%, 45%, 30%), holds the most standards no grade takes to depth, and 5 of the 19 hand-over gaps start from Grade 4 Language standards.

items.title: Talk is our early strength.
items.text: Every Speaking and Listening standard is introduced in Kindergarten and Grade 3, even where nothing reaches depth, and it climbs to 100% in Grades 11 and 12. For students learning English, this could be a natural foundation.

items.title: Foundational reading stops being "in depth" after Grade 2.
items.text: Yet many of our students may still be learning to read in Grades 3 to 5. Phonics and fluency may be taught there below grade level, which the Grade 3 to 5 standards would not show.

items.title: Grade 3 may be teaching more than its rating shows.
items.text: The team kept "in depth" for its Essential Elements (66%) rather than for the grade-level standards. Writing and Speaking and Listening are introduced in full.

items.title: Literacy is also taught in Science and Social Studies.
items.text: These are ELA teams' ratings of ELA lessons. Vocabulary, academic language, speaking and writing are also taught in Science and Social Studies, so ELA standards such as Language and informational reading may be taught more than this part shows. The 2026 literacy audit found about two-fifths of vocabulary teaching, speaking and non-fiction outside the literacy block.

items.title: Kindergarten and Grade 4 rated few standards in depth at either level.
items.text: Their Essential Elements are also rarely in depth (8% and 6%). That sets them apart from Grade 3 and suggests a different explanation, perhaps a stricter reading or a different planning approach.

items.title: Power standards are not yet secure in K-5.
items.text: Kindergarten names 47 power standards; the team has not yet rated any of them in depth, and 62% are not taught yet. In secondary the picture reverses: priorities are in depth more often than ELA as a whole.

items.title: Capacity shows what a grade carries in ELA each year.
items.text: A grade takes about 17 ELA standards to depth a year, introduces about 22 and does not teach about 11, out of about 50 rated. In K-5 it is about 11 of 57, in middle school 23 of 44, in high school 23 of 45. As shares of ELA standards: K-5 19% in depth, 51% introduced, 29% not taught; 6-8 53% in depth, 29% introduced, 18% not taught; 9-12 51% in depth, 42% introduced, 8% not taught. Capacity here means how many standards a grade's teaching time actually holds in a year. It is not a target and not a judgement.

items.title: The SAT road in ELA is well built at the top.
items.text: Reading (61%) and Writing (54%) are strong in high school. Language conventions (30%) may be the area where the SAT asks for more than we currently take to depth.

items.text: That audit found grammar and vocabulary instruction regular in only one or two elementary grades. The ratings agree: Language is the strand most often introduced and never taken to depth.

science.title: Part 7. Science, K-12
science.intro:
Across K-12, teachers reported that 35% of the 247 Science ratings (208 standards) are taught in depth, level with ELA as the highest in the school, and 58% are at least introduced. High school Physical Science (88% in depth) is one of the strongest strands in any subject.

| 6-8 (NGSS) | 74 | 27% | 19% | 54% |
| 9-12 (NGSS) | 83 | 48% | 18% | 34% |
| K-12 | 247 | 35% | 23% | 42% |

items.title: Life Science has a long quiet stretch.
items.text: Strong in K-5 (100% in Grades 2 and 4), then 0% in Grades 6 and 8 and 15% in Grade 7, before returning in Grade 11 (50%). Students may go several years between deep Life Science units.

items.title: Depth alternates from year to year.
items.text: High, low, high, low: 46%, 0%, 50%, 11% in Kindergarten to Grade 3, and 24%, 10%, 43%, 17%, 79% from Grade 6 to Grade 10. Students meet Science in strong years and lighter years. A unit-based plan would produce this pattern, which teams could confirm.

items.title: Physical Science is a through-line worth protecting.
items.text: It builds from 31% to 40% to 88%. But 12 K-5 Physical Science standards are taught by no grade, and 9 hand-over gaps run from those into Grade 8 and Grade 10 Physical Science.

items.title: K-5 progressions are the healthiest in the band.
items.text: Eleven K-5 Science progressions are taught at every step. Where the units exist, they connect.

items.title: Science is also a literacy subject.
items.text: Science units teach vocabulary, informational reading and explanation writing. Teams may be teaching ELA standards in Science that only the ELA ratings would show.

items.title: Science is often all or nothing.
items.text: A standard is usually either in depth or not taught, with little in between (35% in depth, 42% not taught, 23% introduced). One possible reason is that Science is planned in whole units: a topic is either a unit that year or it is not. Grades 1, 4 and 9 are exceptions, with many standards introduced.

items.title: Engineering is taught in bursts.
items.text: It is shared across grade bands (K-2, 3-5, middle, high) and reaches depth in only a few grades. It may be a strand no single grade feels it owns.

items.title: That is a strength with a consequence.
items.text: When Science is taught here, it is taught deeply (Science has the fewest "introduced only" standards: 49, against 105 to 241 in the other subjects). The other side is that coverage depends entirely on which units each grade runs.

items.title: Priority standards are deeper than Science overall.
items.text: Science priority standards are in depth more often than Science overall in every band (37%, 50%, 55%). Grade 7 is the exception (2 of 14).

items.title: Each secondary grade seems to own a discipline.
items.text: Grade 6 Earth and Space, Grade 8 Physical Science and Engineering, Grade 9 Earth and Space, Grade 10 Physical Science, Grade 11 Life Science, and Grade 12 Physical Science (6 of 9 in depth). Grade 7 holds most of the middle school Life Science standards, mostly introduced. Standards placed in a grade that teaches a different discipline show as not taught.

items.title: So much of secondary "not taught" is a placement question.
items.text: There are no confirmed Science gaps in Grades 6 to 12. The 49 standards not taught where placed may simply sit in the wrong year on our map.

items.text: A grade takes about 7 Science standards to depth a year, introduces about 4 and does not teach about 8, out of about 19 rated. Capacity here means how many standards a grade's teaching time actually holds in a year. It is not a target and not a judgement.

social-studies.title: Part 8. Social Studies, K-12
social-studies.intro:
Across K-12, teachers reported that 40% of the 395 Social Studies ratings (225 standards) are at least introduced, and 4% are taught in depth. It is the subject where a few shared choices could make the biggest difference, and it has clear starting points: Kindergarten (40% in depth) and an Economics thread in Grades 6 and 11.

|  | Rated | In depth | Introduced | Not taught |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| K-5 (AERO Social Studies) | 97 | 6% | 30% | 64% |
| 6-8 (Wisconsin) | 192 | 3% | 38% | 59% |
| 9-12 (Wisconsin) | 106 | 3% | 39% | 58% |
| K-12 | 395 | 4% | 36% | 60% |

items.title: Essential Elements (Grades 6 to 12).
items.text: 10% in depth, and 22% in high school against 3% for the main standards.

items.title: Social Studies is consistent across the whole school.
items.text: Unlike the other subjects, it does not rise or dip by band: 6%, 3%, 3% in depth, with about 40% of standards met everywhere. This looks like a whole-school pattern, not the story of any one team.

items.title: Social Studies starts well in Kindergarten.
items.text: Kindergarten's 40% is one of that grade's strongest results, close to Science (46%). Grades 1 to 4 have not yet rated a standard in depth. The question is what changes after Kindergarten.

items.title: Economics shows what a thread can look like.
items.text: In depth in Grade 6, again in Grade 11, with K-5 standards on needs and wants feeding it. It is also where 5 of the 7 hand-over gaps sit: 3 Grade 6 Economics standards build on K-5 standards rated not taught, and 2 Grade 11 standards build on Grade 6.

items.title: Two standard sets meet at Grade 6.
items.text: K-5 uses AERO and Grades 6 to 12 use Wisconsin. The hand-over between them has not been mapped by teachers, only suggested by matching wording.

items.title: Those inquiry skills are close to what ELA already teaches well.
items.text: Research, evidence and argument are in depth in secondary ELA. Social Studies inquiry may be nearer than the ratings suggest, if the two subjects planned together.

items.title: Time may be the simplest explanation.
items.text: With language and reading as the first job in every band, Social Studies may be taught through topics and vocabulary. That fits "introduced" as the usual rating.

items.title: Essential Elements again run ahead in high school.
items.text: In Grade 10, 5 of 9 Essential Elements are in depth while the team has not yet rated a main standard in depth. Deep teaching may be happening at that level.

items.title: Social Studies may be where much literacy happens.

method.title: Method, sources and limits
method.intro:
Every figure in this paper was computed from the ratings sheet and cross-checked against the site. Where the site's band and K-12 views differ (progressions), the paper says which it uses. Percentages are rounded half up, as on the site.

**What was read**

| Source | How it was used | How fully it was read |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ratings sheet, "All Standards and Ratings K-12" (9 Nov 2026) | Every figure | All 2,166 rows |
| Organized ratings workbook | Cross-check of totals | All tabs |
| 20 Findings decks (band and subject) | Cross-check, questions and next-step themes | All slides and speaker notes |
| K-12 Reports PDF (118 pages) | Cross-check | First 80 pages scanned by search; a few read directly |
| 7 other Reports PDFs | Cross-check of headline figures | Scanned by search, not read page by page |

**How terms are used**

- **Rated standards.** One rating is one standard in one grade. A standard shared by several grades is counted once for each grade that rated it.
- **At least introduced.** Rated in depth or introduced.
- **No grade teaches it (confirmed).** Every grade that could teach the standard rated it not taught.
- **Not taught where placed.** The grade it was placed in rated it not taught, and other grades that could teach it were not asked.
- **Introduced, never in depth (met but not owned).** Introduced in at least one grade and in depth in none.
- **Progression finding.** An automatic check on a chain of linked standards: a step not taught, or a standard in depth while the one it builds on is not taught.
- **Taught at every step.** Every standard in the chain, across two or more grades, is at least introduced.
- **Progression.** A chain of linked standards across grades. Official links are the Coherence Map (Math), anchor standards (ELA) and the standards' own structure (Science, Social Studies). Other links are suggestions.
- **Instructional capacity.** The average number of standards one grade rated in depth, introduced and not taught in a year (all ratings divided by the number of grades), rounded.
- **Hand-over gap.** A standard taught in depth while a standard it builds on, placed in an earlier school, is rated not taught.
- **Priority and power standards.** Standards the school's own documents name: power standards in K-5, priority standards in 6-12.

**Limits to keep in view**

- Ratings are teachers' judgements of teaching across a grade. They are not observations and not student results.
- Grades may have read "in depth" differently. Uniform ratings across a whole grade are a reason to check how the scale was read; the paper points these out so teams can discuss them.
- The ratings are what teachers reported as taught. They do not measure what students know or can do.
- Each team rated its own subject. Literacy taught in Science and Social Studies, and Math taught in Science, may not show in the ELA and Math ratings.
- Middle school Science and high school standards were placed in grades and courses by suggestion. "Not taught" there can mean "taught in another year". 24 K-5 Social Studies standards are also not taught in the grade where they were placed.
- Band counts of progressions look only at steps inside the band, so they do not add up to the K-12 figure.
- Literacy audit figures come from the 2026 PK-5 literacy audit of weekly plans.
- Some strands have few standards in a grade, so a single rating can move a percentage a long way. Counts are given where this matters.
- Suggested links between standards (most ELA, Science and Social Studies hand-overs) have not been checked by teachers.

**Status.** This is a draft for the Vertical Alignment Committee. Each finding should be checked with the teams concerned before it is treated as settled. The planned review of weekly and unit plans (Part 2) will test many of these patterns against what is actually planned.

see.patterns: What we notice when we put the facts side by side: rises, dips and comparisons. These are possibilities to talk about, not conclusions.
see.questions: Questions for teams to talk about. Each one shows the data that prompted it, and links to where that figure appears on this page.
see.ourpart: Options for what we could do, under four headings, each with the data behind it.

whole.glance: Most of what we teach is introduced. ELA and Science go deepest, and Social Studies is where we have the most room to grow.
whole.grades: Depth goes up and down from grade to grade rather than climbing steadily, so the hand-overs between grades matter.
whole.data: For the first time we have a complete picture: every rating is in, and it shows real strengths and places to build.
whole.patterns: Coverage is steady across the school; what changes is how far we take things. That points us toward choosing what to go deep on.
whole.questions: This is where the story turns to us: what we choose to protect, and how grades can work together.
whole.table: The gap between subjects is the widest thing in the table: 4% in depth in Social Studies against 35% in ELA and Science.

k-5.glance: K-5 introduces widely. Math and Science go deepest, and Social Studies is mostly still to come.
k-5.grades: Grade 2 shows how deep teaching can go. The grades around it rated more cautiously, which is worth talking about together.
k-5.data: The foundations are strong in number and early reading. Fractions, Language and Social Studies are the thinner threads.
k-5.patterns: Much deep teaching in K-5 may happen at the level students are at (the Essential Elements), which the main ratings do not show.
k-5.questions: K-5 sets up everything that follows, so these questions are about what every child carries into Grade 6.
k-5.table: Grade 2 carries the most depth in three subjects, and Social Studies is light after Kindergarten. Each team can find its own cell.

g6-8.glance: ELA is the strength of middle school. Math covers almost everything and has not yet rated a standard in depth.
g6-8.grades: Each middle school grade has its own mix, and Science seems to give each grade its own discipline.
g6-8.data: Two very different pictures sit side by side here, which makes middle school a good place to compare how teams read the scale.
g6-8.patterns: Many differences here may come from how courses are scheduled and how strictly "in depth" was read, not from how much is taught.
g6-8.questions: Middle school is the bridge between two schools, so these questions are about what students bring in and carry on.
g6-8.table: ELA is strong in every middle school grade, while Math and Social Studies are mostly introduced. Each team can find its own cell.

g9-12.glance: High school goes deepest of the three bands, led by ELA and Science.
g9-12.grades: ELA builds year on year, and Math is strongest in Grade 9. The picture is mostly about choices between courses.
g9-12.data: Few standards are missing everywhere. Most open questions are about which course teaches what.
g9-12.patterns: Steady, planned sequences (like ELA) lead to depth, and the SAT areas in Math deserve a closer look.
g9-12.questions: These questions are about the end of the journey: what every graduate should leave with.
g9-12.table: ELA and Science grow through high school, and Math is strongest in Grade 9. Each team can find its own cell.

math.glance: Math introduces most of its standards. Depth is strongest in K-5 and in Grade 9.
math.grades: Strong early grades and a strong Grade 9 frame the middle years, where Math is introduced rather than taken to depth.
math.data: Number is our strength. Fractions, ratios and equations, the path to algebra, are the thread to follow.
math.patterns: Following one idea, such as fractions to equations, across the grades shows where students may need more depth.
math.questions: These questions ask how Math teams across grades could agree on a few standards to take deeper together.
math.table: Middle school introduces almost all its Math, and high school leaves the most not taught, often by course choice.

ela.glance: ELA has the widest coverage and the most depth of any subject.
ela.grades: ELA grows strongly from K-5 into secondary, with a few grades that rated more cautiously.
ela.data: Reading, writing and talk are strengths. Language (grammar and vocabulary) is the thread to strengthen, and much of it may be taught in other subjects.
ela.patterns: ELA shows what steady building across grades looks like, and that literacy also lives in Science and Social Studies.
ela.questions: These questions are about sharing what works in ELA and deciding who takes Language to depth.
ela.table: "Not taught" shrinks from 29% in K-5 to 8% in high school: by the end, ELA reaches nearly everything.

science.glance: Science is often all or nothing: a topic is either taught deeply or not taught that year.
science.grades: Depth changes from year to year, which may simply follow which units each grade runs.
science.data: When Science is taught, it is taught deeply. The open question is which year each topic lives in.
science.patterns: Much of "not taught" in secondary Science may be a placement question, and Science also carries a lot of literacy.
science.questions: These questions are about a shared K-12 map of Science units, so every strand has a home.
science.table: Each band takes between a quarter and a half of its Science to depth. Middle school leaves the most not taught, often a placement question.

social-studies.glance: Social Studies is mostly introduced. This is where a few shared choices could make the biggest difference.
social-studies.grades: Kindergarten starts strongly. After that Social Studies is mostly introduced, perhaps because much of the time goes to literacy.
social-studies.data: Topics are met across the school, and Economics shows what a thread taught to depth can look like.
social-studies.patterns: Social Studies may be where much of our literacy happens, so planning the two together could help both.
social-studies.questions: These questions are about choosing a few Social Studies standards per grade to take deeper, often through literacy we already teach.
social-studies.table: The same pattern holds in every band: about four in ten introduced and very little in depth.
